description: We are a team of passionate innovators interested in combining AI, software engineering, and space exploration to solve real-world challenges. With experience in computer science, machine learning, and data analysis, we aim to build an ambitious, impactful NASA Space Apps project. We welcome creative problem-solvers with skills in coding, AI/ML, data visualization, astronomy, UI/UX, and research. Whether you're experienced or eager to learn, we'd love to collaborate!
summary:
Lunaris is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform developed by Team Pitzer Connect to help researchers, students, and space enthusiasts explore candidate sites near the Moon's south pole.

Using NASA JPL Horizons astronomical data and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain information, Lunaris analyzes sunlight availability, Earth visibility, terrain obstructions, and potential communication outages.

Users can compare lunar locations, select mission dates and observation heights, explore mission windows of up to 30 days, and visualize periods of darkness and Earth visibility. The platform also offers terrain-aware horizon modeling, smooth-sphere comparisons, date-window comparisons, and terrain slope screening.

By translating complex NASA datasets into accessible interactive visualizations, Lunaris helps users understand how local topography, sunlight, and communication opportunities influence lunar mission planning.

Lunaris is an educational and research prototype designed to support informed exploration, not a certified landing-site selection system.
details:
The Problem

Exploring the Moon's south pole presents significant mission-planning challenges. Because the Sun remains low on the horizon, mountains and crater rims can create extended periods of darkness. The surrounding terrain can also obstruct direct visibility of Earth, affecting opportunities for communication.

Choosing a lunar location therefore requires understanding how illumination, terrain, time, and observation height interact. Although NASA provides valuable scientific datasets, interpreting and comparing this information can be difficult for students, educators, and early-stage researchers.

Our Solution: Lunaris

Team Pitzer Connect developed Lunaris: Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Navigator, an interactive web application that helps users investigate environmental conditions at candidate sites near the lunar south pole.

Lunaris combines NASA astronomical data with lunar terrain information to make mission-planning tradeoffs easier to explore and visualize.

Key Features

1. Lunar Site Selection and Comparison

Users can select candidate lunar locations and compare their environmental conditions. This helps reveal differences in sunlight and Earth visibility between sites.

2. Terrain-Aware Horizon Analysis

Lunaris uses lunar elevation information to estimate how surrounding terrain can obstruct the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth.

3. NASA JPL Horizons Integration

Our backend retrieves astronomical positions from NASA JPL Horizons and processes them into data that can be explored through the web interface.

4. Mission-Window Analysis

Users can examine mission windows ranging from 1 to 30 days, explore changing visibility conditions, and identify sampled periods of darkness and Earth visibility.

5. Communication and Illumination Insights

The application summarizes potential Earth-visibility interruptions and periods of darkness, helping users recognize environmental tradeoffs that may influence mission planning.

6. Adjustable Observation Height

Users can investigate how different observation heights influence modeled visibility conditions.

7. Terrain vs. Smooth-Sphere Comparison

Lunaris allows users to compare terrain-aware estimates with a simplified smooth-sphere model, illustrating why local lunar topography matters.

8. Date-Window Comparison and Terrain Screening

Users can compare consecutive mission windows and examine terrain slope information as an additional research consideration.

9. Accessible Visual Interface

Interactive charts, lunar imagery, responsive layouts, and light/dark modes make the platform easier to explore on different devices.

Technical Implementation

Lunaris uses the following technologies:

  • React and TypeScript: Interactive user interface and scientific visualizations.
  • Vite: Frontend development and production builds.
  • Python and FastAPI: Backend API and processing of astronomical and terrain-related information.
  • NASA JPL Horizons: Astronomical position data.
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA: Lunar topographic information.
  • NASA LROC WAC imagery: Geographic context for lunar south-pole exploration.
  • GitHub: Version control and team collaboration.
  • Vercel: Frontend deployment.
  • Render: Backend deployment.

What Makes Lunaris Innovative?

Lunaris brings together time-dependent astronomical positions, lunar terrain analysis, and interactive site comparisons in one accessible interface.

Instead of requiring users to interpret multiple scientific data sources independently, Lunaris organizes the results into comparative charts, mission timelines, and visibility summaries.

The ability to explore observation heights, mission dates, terrain obstructions, and alternative lunar locations helps users understand the complexity of lunar environmental planning.

Intended Impact

Lunaris is designed for students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts who want to investigate the environmental challenges of lunar exploration.

Our goal is to make NASA scientific data more approachable, encourage learning about lunar mission planning, and provide an accessible foundation for further research and educational development.

Scientific Limitations

Lunaris is an educational and research prototype, not a certified landing-site selection or operational mission-planning system.

Predictions are limited by the resolution and accuracy of the source data and the model's assumptions. Sun visibility does not guarantee sufficient electrical power, and direct Earth visibility does not guarantee reliable communications. The application does not perform a comprehensive landing-hazard assessment, detailed communications link budget, or full spacecraft mission feasibility evaluation.

Candidate locations are research reference points rather than approved landing coordinates.
